propositions.text: The claimants are Guatemalan citizens seeking protection under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

paragraphs.summary: The claimants are Guatemalan citizens seeking protection under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, stated by the court.

propositions.text: The mother was appointed as the designated representative of her son.

paragraphs.summary: The mother was appointed as the designated representative of her son, stated by the court.

propositions.text: The female claimant was a vendor affected by organized crime involving police commanders, political officials, and customs officers.
These officials lived off corruption and impunity profits.

paragraphs.summary: The female claimant alleges organized crime involving officials profiting from corruption, stated by the applicant.

propositions.text: In 2000, organized crime members extorted 1,000 quetzals monthly from her to continue working.
This extortion applied to all merchant citizens.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges extortion of 1,000 quetzals monthly by organized crime in 2000, affecting all merchants.

propositions.text: She reported extortion to police who never appeared.
Her husband reported to public ministry but was told to report at time of intimidation for investigation.
Authorities said they could not protect her 24 hours a day.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges police did not respond to reports and authorities could not provide full protection, stated by the applicant.

propositions.text: She collected signatures and led groups paying and not paying extortion.
She sent three lists to police accusing authorities of complicity and blaming them for the situation.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges she led groups and sent lists accusing authorities of complicity in organized crime.

propositions.text: She moved to another sector to sell.
In 2000, criminal investigation officers came to her home to question her as an example to others.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges she moved and was questioned by criminal officers as an example, stated by the applicant.

propositions.text: She left the country in 2000 to escape criminals who wanted to stop her.
She feared returning to the US because she was employed in her country of origin.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges she left the country to escape criminals and feared returning to the US due to employment.

propositions.text: In 2005, her husband returned to Guatemala to get a work visa but left after a week due to threatening calls.
Threatening calls continued after he left, forcing his brother to relocate.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges her husband faced threats in 2005 and his brother had to relocate due to continued threats.

propositions.text: The female claimant fears returning to Guatemala because of criminals.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant fears returning to Guatemala due to criminals, stated by the applicant.

propositions.text: Exhibit A-2,1 with passports identifies claimants to the panel's satisfaction.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimants' identity established by passport exhibits.

propositions.text: The testimony was not credible; the female claimant alleged extortionists disguised to avoid recognition.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the female claimant's testimony not credible regarding disguised extortionists.

propositions.text: The female claimant was a street vendor who also sold at clients' homes, with volunteers purchasing merchandise.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the female claimant sold merchandise at clients' homes with volunteers purchasing.

propositions.text: She stated receiving six calls between two dates in 2000, with extortionists forcing payment within three days.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant stated six calls in 2000 with extortionists demanding payment within three days.

propositions.text: The panel and claimant situated calls as occurring three or four times a day.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds calls occurred three or four times daily, as situated by panel and claimant.

propositions.text: She allegedly received calls on specific dates and times, including many calls on her cellphone.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant alleged multiple calls on specific dates and times, including many on her cellphone.

propositions.text: On a date in 2000, three individuals warned her; she went to police who told her to call when gang was present.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant was warned by individuals and police advised her to call when gang was present.

propositions.text: The claimant gave inconsistent dates for the last call and eventually said she did not remember well.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant gave inconsistent dates for the last call and poor memory of dates.

propositions.text: It is normal to mistake dates after 12 years, but claimant earlier recalled details well.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it normal to mistake dates after 12 years but claimant previously recalled details well.

propositions.text: The panel rejects the claimant's dates as fabricated and not in her PIF, noting contradictions.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the claimant's dates as fabricated and contradictory to her PIF statements.

propositions.text: Calls allegedly continued until XXXX XXXX, but testimony says calls stopped by XXXX or XXXX, 2000.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes calls allegedly continued until XXXX XXXX, but testimony says calls stopped by XXXX or XXXX, 2000.

propositions.text: There were about 30 days when the claimant did not receive calls at all.
Claimant's story says calls continued until XXXX, but testimony says calls stopped on XXXX or XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds about 30 days without calls; claimant says calls continued until XXXX, but testimony says calls stopped on XXXX or XXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant tried to present herself as a female leader mobilizing merchants and torchbearer for merchants.
It is implausible that a street vendor could mobilize merchants with stores not to pay Maras.
More plausible she mobilized other street vendors, not merchants with stores.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant portrayed herself as a leader but it is implausible she mobilized merchants with stores; more plausible she mobilized street vendors.

propositions.text: The panel does not believe the claimant was able to mobilize the merchants as she claims.

paragraphs.summary: The panel does not believe claimant was able to mobilize merchants as claimed.

propositions.text: Claimant said she acted alone and went to police alone, but PIF says 'we sent...', indicating a group.
Claimant had no response to this inconsistency about group involvement.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's claim of acting alone contradicted by PIF indicating group involvement; claimant gave no response.

propositions.text: Even if credible, claimant faced generalized violence; Maras demand ransoms from entire population.
Claim that she was targeted for reporting is very general and not credible.
Claimant said police needed descriptions or names to proceed when called anonymously or disguised.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant faced generalized violence; claim of targeting for reporting is general and not credible; police needed descriptions or names to act.

propositions.text: Claimant never gave details to identify extortionists or crooked police officers allegedly colluding with gang.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant never gave details to identify extortionists or crooked police officers allegedly colluding with gang.

propositions.text: Since claimant did not identify responsible people, panel does not believe criminal investigation officers came looking for her as claimed.

paragraphs.summary: The panel does not believe criminal investigation officers came looking for claimant because she did not identify responsible people.

propositions.text: Claimant submitted documents reporting extortion but they do not identify anyone.
Report is general, does not enable arrest or vengeance.
Claimant talked about offenders in Exhibit A-2 but did not mention reporting them or police involvement.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant submitted extortion reports that do not identify anyone; report is general and does not enable arrest; claimant did not mention reporting offenders or police.

propositions.text: Claimant said no space to mention reporting police and criminals, but panel does not accept this explanation.
Claimant's refugee claim text describes extortion generally and took more space than a short mention of reporting would.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant said no space to mention reporting police, but court rejects this; claimant's claim text describes extortion generally and took more space.

propositions.text: Claimant's husband acknowledged fleeing to US urgently due to extortionist gangs' threats while visiting ill mother in Guatemala.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant's husband fled to US urgently due to extortionist gangs' threats while visiting ill mother in Guatemala.

propositions.text: Claimants stayed in US for many years, entered illegally, and exceeded refugee claim deadline.
They made inquiries and received a response about their status.
Panel opines claimants failed to discharge burden of proof.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants stayed illegally in US, exceeded refugee claim deadline, made inquiries, and panel finds they failed to discharge burden of proof.

propositions.text: Designated representative did not submit evidence against US, son's country of citizenship.

paragraphs.summary: Designated representative did not submit evidence against US, son's country of citizenship.

propositions.text: Claimant, spouse, and son are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant, spouse, and son are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
